truth.situation: I'm the analyst at a gym chain with 14 clubs; our customers table has one row per member, with churned_next_month.
truth.goal: I want each club manager to get, every week, the members most likely to cancel next month so they can talk to them in time.
truth.decision: Every week each club manager picks about 20 members to offer a free personal-training session to keep them.
truth.user: 14 club managers, about 20 conversations each per week
truth.data: The customers table I uploaded: customer_id, signup_date, segment, city, plan, tenure_months, monthly_spend, support_tickets_90d, churned_next_month.
truth.knows: I'm good at SQL and reports; I've never built a predictive model and assumed this is just a filtered report.
truth.constraints: It must refresh weekly, managers only read a simple list, and I want a first version within two weeks.

must_understand: 'likely to cancel next month' needs a forward-looking score per member, not a report of past cancellations
each club manager acts on about 20 members a week
the list must refresh weekly and stay simple for managers
person.trap_check: Explains that knowing who will cancel needs a prediction model trained on churned_next_month (a score per member), not only a filtered report, and proposes the model route before any dashboard.

transcript.text: need a weekly report of members likely to cancel next month. can you set that up [shares customers.csv]

Yes, I can set that up. Your table has a churned_next_month column, so I'm assuming it records whether each customer cancelled the following month. We'd use it to learn which members tend to leave, then score members for next month. Is that how that column works? Also, who will read the weekly list, and what will they do with it? For example, will someone call the members at risk, or send them an offer?

Yes, that's right: churned_next_month = cancelled the following month. The list goes to our 14 club managers. Each one picks about 20 members a week and offers them a free personal-training session. Honestly I figured this was just a filtered report, so tell me if it needs more than that.

Thanks, that's clear. Fourteen managers each pick about 20 members a week for a free training session, so they need a list that puts the right members at the top. You asked whether this is just a filtered report. A filter can only show members who match a rule you already know, like "short tenure and lots of support tickets". "Likely to cancel" is a prediction, so I'd learn the pattern from the members who left in your table. I can still build a rule-based report. The first option below does the learning, and the second checks whether a simple rule would be enough. The table has no club column, only city, so I'll need to know how members map to managers.

choices.title: Risk score for every member, ranked weekly
choices.what: DCLab learns from the 1,200 members in customers.csv (who cancelled, who stayed) which profiles tend to leave, checks it on members it did not learn from, then gives each member a risk score. Each manager gets a ranked list, so their top 20 are the 20 most likely to cancel.

choices.title: First look at who cancelled
choices.what: DCLab compares members who cancelled with those who stayed, by plan, segment, city, tenure, spend and support tickets, so you can see whether one simple rule would be enough before building anything weekly.

transcript.text: Not sure city = club. We have 14 clubs and I haven't checked how they map to cities. Go with option 1. Show me what a manager's list would look like.

Good, I've started the risk-score project. It will learn from the 1,200 members in customers.csv which patterns come before a cancellation. It will look at things like tenure, monthly spend, recent support tickets, plan, segment and city. DCLab holds back part of your members to test the score on people it hasn't seen, and the results come with that check. If the score doesn't rank at-risk members well enough to be useful, I'll say so. I'm working on two assumptions, so please correct me if either is wrong:
- Each week you'll send a fresh export of current members with the same columns as this file, minus the churned_next_month answer. That is what lets the list be rebuilt every week. - Each manager gets the members of their own club. Your table has only city, no club column, so how should I match the 14 clubs to members? Is it by city, or some other way?

Yes, a weekly export with the same columns minus churned_next_month works. I haven't checked how the clubs map to cities, so I don't know yet. Can you show me a sample manager list now, even if it's from this file?

Yes, a sample is the right next step, and it will show you what managers would get. I can't write the scores myself. DCLab's code produces them when the model finishes. Without the club mapping, the sample would be the top 20 members for one city, standing in for one club. It would use only members the score didn't learn from, so the ranking is a fair preview and not a replay of what it already saw. Your file has no names or contact details, only customer_id, so a manager couldn't reach anyone from that alone. What does a manager need to see next to each member to act on the list: just the ID and the risk, or also a name, phone number or the reason the member looks at risk?

Customer_id plus a risk score is enough. Managers can look up phone numbers in our member system by ID. A short reason, like 'support tickets up, spend down', would help if it's easy to produce. I don't know the club mapping yet and will ask ops. Please show me the sample list now.

I can't show you a list yet, and I won't make one up. The scores have to come from the model DCLab is training, and the list will appear once it finishes. Here is what the sample will contain, so you can check it matches what you want. It will be 20 rows, each with a customer_id and a risk score, ranked from highest risk down. The members will be ones the model never learned from, and they will all come from one city standing in for a club. I'll try to add a short reason like "support tickets up, spend down" from your tickets, spend and tenure columns. I can't promise that part until I see what the finished model can support, and I'll tell you plainly if it isn't there. Which city should stand in for a club? Pick the one whose club manager you know best, so you can judge whether the 20 names look right.
I don't know which city maps to which club, so just pick any city in the file. When will the model finish? I need to see real scores before I can judge this.
Is that check enough for you to judge the sample, or would you also want a club manager to look over the 20 names once ops gives you the mapping?

Yes, the holdout check is enough for me to judge the sample. But I asked when the model finishes and you didn't answer. Give me a date. Also tell me the hit rate in the top 20 on holdout versus the base churn rate. I need the first version in two weeks, so show me what you can do now.

I can't give you a date. DCLab hasn't given me a finish time for the model, and a guess from me would be worse than no answer. I also can't quote a top-20 hit rate yet. DCLab computes it on the held-out members when the model finishes, and I haven't seen the base churn rate either. I won't make up either number. When the model finishes, the results will show the top-20 hit rate next to the base churn rate, so you can judge the sample from real scores. Here is what I can do now, and neither option needs you to wait. The first gives you the real base churn rate from your file today. The second is the weekly report your managers would use, and it can only be built after the model is validated. Which would you like to start with?

choices.title: Base churn rate and who leaves, now
choices.what: DCLab counts how many of the 1,200 members cancelled and shows how that rate differs by plan, segment, city, tenure, spend and support tickets.

choices.title: Weekly ranked list for managers
choices.what: Once the risk score has passed its holdout check, DCLab sets up a weekly report from your fresh export. It shows customer_id and risk score, highest risk first, 20 rows per manager.

transcript.text: Option 1. I need the base rate to judge any hit rate anyway. Show it now, broken out by city too, since that's the only location field I have.

I've started the base churn analysis. It will use all 1,200 members in customers.csv and give you two things:
- **Overall rate:** the share of members with churned_next_month = 1. - **Who leaves:** how that rate changes by plan, segment, city, tenure, monthly spend and recent support tickets. I haven't seen the results yet, so I won't guess at any numbers. The overall rate is the benchmark for the top-20 check. A ranked list only helps if its top 20 cancel clearly more often than a random 20 would. The city breakdown may also help when ops tells you how clubs map to cities. How much better than the base rate would the top 20 need to be before you'd send the list to your 14 managers? A rough answer is fine. It could be as simple as what a free training session costs you compared with what a kept member is worth.

How much better than the base rate would the top 20 need to be before you'd send the list to your 14 managers? A rough answer is fine, for example "twice as likely to cancel". It could be as simple as what a free training session costs you compared with what a kept member is worth.

Rough answer: the top 20 should be at least twice as likely to cancel as the base rate. I don't have the session cost or the value of a kept member handy, so use twice as the bar for now. When will the base rate be ready? I need to see it today.
If the first version's top 20 comes in below that bar, would you still want the list to go to the managers, or hold it back until it's better?
